title: Adaptive grace-window eviction broker for prefix-safe GPU memory compaction
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Continuous batching and aggressive GPU memory compaction are causing short-lived but severe cache churn on multi-tenant serving nodes. When large batched requests complete, many prefixes become cold simultaneously and naive LRU/TTL eviction combined with compaction causes prefix thrashing, higher tail latency, and correctness hazards (evicting KV entries still referenced by in-flight batches).

Goal: Implement an adaptive 'eviction broker' that mediates reclamation across tenants and batches using a tunable grace-window and pin/lease mechanism to guarantee prefix consistency while enabling efficient GPU memory compaction. The broker should provide formal invariants (no eviction of pinned prefixes, bounded reclamation latency) and be deployable incrementally via canary and A/B rollout.

Scope: runtime allocator and KV lease manager changes, batch lifecycle annotation in request path, eviction policy shim implementing grace-window hysteresis, metrics and dashboards, property tests and fuzzing harnesses. Not in scope: wholesale allocator redesign, cross-region global eviction coordination (future work).
acceptance_criteria: Property tests show no eviction of pinned prefixes in 100k simulated batch lifecycles
End-to-end perf: 95th percentile token latency within 5% of baseline under representative continuous-batching workloads
Memory compaction achieves >=12% reduction in peak GPU memory usage on mixed TTL/LRU workloads without increased tail error rates
Automated rollback trigger defined and validated (safety net) in Console with clear SLO thresholds
Integration tests pass on CI and a staged canary in dedicated-1 cluster with runtime-1.19
technical_notes: Design: eviction broker maintains per-tenant soft quotas and a per-batch pin registry. Pins are short-lived leases (epoch+lease-id) tied to batch lifecycle; eviction code must consult broker before reclaiming any slot referenced by active lease.

Grace-window: when a prefix becomes cold, it enters a grace state for configurable ms (default 120ms) to allow burst completion and avoid immediate eviction; multiple grace-window extensions allowed up to a cap using access heuristics.
Correctness invariants: (1) pins are monotonic per-batch; (2) eviction never reclaims a slot with an active pin; (3) lease revocation uses epoch counters to avoid ABA issues during reallocation.

Fallback policy: under severe pressure, broker can transition tenants into TTL-only reclamation with a bias toward high-frequency prefixes (soft-deprioritization); thresholds based on eviction_rate and inflight_batch_count metrics.

Performance trade-offs: pins and grace windows increase short-term memory usage and allocator bookkeeping; however they reduce thrash and tail latency. We'll quantify cost in perf runs and expose config per-tenant for Dedicated customers.

Implementation pieces: (a) KV lease manager module (C++ runtime) with thin RPC hooks; (b) batch lifecycle tagging in dispatcher/worker (Go) to acquire/release leases; (c) eviction broker state sharded by GPU slab; (d) metrics: broker_pins, grace_window_extensions, eviction_skips_due_to_pin, eviction_rate_by_tenant.
Hardening: add deterministic simulation harness (fuzzbench extension) that replays production traces with injected concurrency and fault modes; run for 72h across varied config space.

Rollout: feature flag with three modes (disabled / grace-window-only / full-broker). Start canary on 2% traffic in dedicated cluster, monitor eviction_skips, p95 latency, error-rate; escalate if >10% regression on p95 or increased errors.
progress_updates: 2026-02-16: Kickoff meeting with Runtime and Serving teams. Agreed high-level API surface for lease manager. Action items: PRD + simulation plan (Maya), initial runtime API sketch (Omar).
2026-02-22: Runtime API sketch posted: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Lease+Manager+API. Decided to use epoch counters to avoid race conditions when renewing leases.

2026-03-01: Prototype in C++ runtime: basic pin/lease registration + eviction gating. Local microbench shows ~2% overhead on small synthetic traces. Pushed branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/2891.

2026-03-05: Simulation run #1 (fuzzbench) completed: observed reduction in eviction-induced tail latency by 18% on mixed workloads. Identified bug: double-free path when lease revocation raced with compaction GC; added unit to cover this.

2026-03-10: Integration test harness wired to CI; added Console metrics and dashboard draft: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/kv/eviction-broker-canary (draft). Planning canary for 2026-03-20 in dedicated-1 cluster.
Next: finalize PR addressing race fix, add property tests, and schedule canary with SRE.
tests: Property-based invariants: generate batch lifecycles and assert no eviction of pinned slots (100k runs)
Deterministic replay: replay sampled production traces with continuous-batching and measure p50/p95/p99 latency
Fuzzbench: inject lease revocation races and compaction GC with random timings
Integration: end-to-end serving test with canary traffic in dedicated-1 cluster
Load: synthetic high-concurrency run to validate memory compaction effectiveness and cost impact
notes: Consider exposing per-tenant grace-window tuning in Console for Dedicated customers to balance cost vs tail latency.
Long-term: evaluate combining broker with prefetch hints from prompt router to proactively pin hot prefixes during expected bursts.
If successful, can form the basis for a cross-shard eviction policy (phase 2) that coordinates across GPU-bound shards in a node.
